items.followUp: How does atomic size change down a group, and how does this affect an atom’s tendency to lose an electron?

rubric.why: Identifies the direction of the trend.
rubric.description: Electropositivity increases down a group.
rubric.how: State the trend down the group.

rubric.why: Explains the trend using the easier loss of an outer electron.
rubric.description: Increasing atomic size and shielding reduce the attraction between the nucleus and the outermost electron, so it is lost more easily.
rubric.how: Link increased size or shielding with weaker nuclear attraction and easier electron loss.

modelAnswer: Electropositivity increases down a group in the periodic table.
Down the group, atomic size and shielding effect increase, so the nucleus attracts the outermost electron less strongly.
Therefore, the outermost electron is lost more easily.

items.followUp: State two uses of sodium and briefly describe each use.

rubric.why: Gives one valid use of sodium.
rubric.description: Sodium is used in sodium-vapour lamps for street lighting.
rubric.how: Name sodium-vapour lamps or street lighting.

rubric.why: Gives another valid use of sodium.
rubric.description: Sodium is used as a coolant in nuclear reactors.
rubric.how: Name its use as a nuclear-reactor coolant.

modelAnswer: Sodium is used in sodium-vapour lamps for street lighting.
It is used as a coolant in nuclear reactors.

items.followUp: State Bohr’s postulates for the arrangement and movement of electrons in an atom.

rubric.why: States the basic arrangement of electrons in Bohr’s model.
rubric.description: Electrons revolve around the nucleus in definite circular orbits or shells.
rubric.how: Mention electrons revolving around the nucleus in definite orbits.

rubric.why: Identifies the energy of the allowed orbits.
rubric.description: Each permitted orbit has a fixed, definite energy.
rubric.how: State that an electron in an allowed orbit has a definite energy.

rubric.why: Distinguishes a stationary orbit from an electron transition.
rubric.description: An electron in a permitted stationary orbit does not radiate or lose energy.
rubric.how: State that an electron does not radiate energy while in an allowed orbit.

rubric.why: Describes how an electron changes energy levels.
rubric.description: An electron absorbs or emits energy when it jumps between orbits.
rubric.how: Mention absorption or emission of energy during a transition between orbits.

rubric.why: Gives the energy condition for an electron transition.
rubric.description: The energy absorbed or emitted equals the difference between the energies of the two orbits: ΔE = hν.
rubric.how: Write the relation between the energy difference and the frequency of radiation.

modelAnswer: Bohr’s atomic theory states that electrons revolve around the nucleus in definite circular orbits called shells.
Each permitted orbit has a fixed energy, and an electron in it does not radiate energy.
An electron absorbs or emits energy only when it jumps from one orbit to another.
The energy absorbed or emitted is equal to the difference between the energies of the two orbits: ΔE = hν.
The angular momentum of an electron in an allowed orbit is quantized: mvr = nh/2π, where n is a whole number.

items.followUp: Give four differences between an element and a compound.

rubric.why: Compares the composition of compounds and mixtures.
rubric.description: A compound has elements in a fixed ratio, whereas a mixture can have components in any proportion.
rubric.how: State the fixed ratio in compounds and variable proportions in mixtures.

rubric.why: Compares the properties of the constituents and the resulting material.
rubric.description: A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements; components of a mixture retain their properties.
rubric.how: Contrast the changed properties in compounds with retained properties in mixtures.

rubric.why: Compares methods of separation.
rubric.description: A compound is separated into its elements by chemical methods; a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
rubric.how: Identify chemical separation for compounds and physical separation for mixtures.

rubric.why: Compares representation of composition.
rubric.description: A compound has a definite chemical formula; a mixture has no fixed formula.
rubric.how: State that compounds have formulae while mixtures do not have a fixed formula.

modelAnswer: A compound contains elements chemically combined in a fixed ratio; a mixture may contain its components in any proportion.
A compound has properties different from those of its constituent elements; the components of a mixture retain their individual properties.
A compound can be separated into its elements by chemical methods; a mixture can be separated by physical methods.
A compound has a definite chemical formula; a mixture has no fixed chemical formula.

items.followUp: What is hydrogen bonding? Explain its occurrence between water molecules.

rubric.why: Defines the interaction between permanent dipoles.
rubric.description: Dipole-dipole interaction is the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ends of polar molecules.
rubric.how: Define it as attraction between the positive end of one polar molecule and the negative end of another.

rubric.why: Identifies the polar ends of HCl molecules.
rubric.description: In HCl, hydrogen is partially positive and chlorine is partially negative.
rubric.how: Show the polarity of HCl as Hδ+—Clδ− or equivalent.

rubric.why: Applies the interaction to neighbouring HCl molecules.
rubric.description: The Hδ+ end of one HCl molecule is attracted to the Clδ− end of another.
rubric.how: Describe the attraction between opposite ends of adjacent HCl molecules.

rubric.why: Identifies the nature of the interaction.
rubric.description: The interaction acts between separate HCl molecules.
rubric.how: State that the attraction is intermolecular.

modelAnswer: Dipole-dipole interaction is the electrostatic attraction between the oppositely charged ends of neighbouring polar molecules.
In an HCl molecule, hydrogen has a partial positive charge and chlorine has a partial negative charge: Hδ+—Clδ−.
The Hδ+ end of one HCl molecule attracts the Clδ− end of a neighbouring HCl molecule.
This attraction between separate HCl molecules is a dipole-dipole interaction.

items.followUp: Explain how temperature and the nature of a liquid affect its vapour pressure.

rubric.why: Identifies the effect of temperature.
rubric.description: Vapour pressure increases as temperature increases.
rubric.how: State the direction of the change with increasing temperature.

rubric.why: Explains the temperature effect.
rubric.description: At higher temperature, molecules have more kinetic energy and more escape into the vapour phase.
rubric.how: Link increased temperature to greater molecular kinetic energy and evaporation.

rubric.why: Identifies the effect of the liquid’s nature.
rubric.description: Vapour pressure depends on the strength of intermolecular forces in the liquid.
rubric.how: Mention the liquid’s nature or its intermolecular forces.

rubric.why: Explains how intermolecular forces affect vapour pressure.
rubric.description: Stronger intermolecular forces hold molecules more tightly and lower vapour pressure; weaker forces result in higher vapour pressure.
rubric.how: Give the correct relationship between intermolecular-force strength and vapour pressure.

modelAnswer: Vapour pressure depends on the temperature and the nature of the liquid.
When temperature increases, the kinetic energy of liquid molecules increases, so more molecules escape into the vapour phase and vapour pressure rises.
The nature of a liquid affects the strength of the intermolecular forces between its molecules.
Stronger intermolecular forces make it harder for molecules to escape, giving a lower vapour pressure; weaker forces give a higher vapour pressure.

items.followUp: Define saturated, unsaturated, concentrated and dilute solutions, giving one example of each.

rubric.why: Explains one type of solution by its capacity to dissolve more solute.
rubric.description: An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at a given temperature; for example, a small amount of salt dissolved in water.
rubric.how: Define an unsaturated solution and give a suitable example.

rubric.why: Explains the solution at its solubility limit.
rubric.description: A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature; for example, saturated salt solution.
rubric.how: Define a saturated solution and give a suitable example.

rubric.why: Explains a solution containing a relatively large amount of solute.
rubric.description: A concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute compared with the solvent; for example, concentrated sugar solution.
rubric.how: Define a concentrated solution and give a suitable example.

rubric.why: Explains a solution containing a relatively small amount of solute.
rubric.description: A dilute solution contains a relatively small amount of solute compared with the solvent; for example, dilute sugar solution.
rubric.how: Define a dilute solution and give a suitable example.

modelAnswer: An unsaturated solution can dissolve more solute at a given temperature; for example, a small amount of salt dissolved in water.
A saturated solution contains the maximum amount of solute that can dissolve at a given temperature; for example, saturated salt solution.
A concentrated solution contains a relatively large amount of solute compared with the solvent; for example, concentrated sugar solution.
A dilute solution contains a relatively small amount of solute compared with the solvent; for example, dilute sugar solution.

items.followUp: Give one example each of a homogeneous mixture and a heterogeneous mixture, and state how they differ in composition.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining composition of a homogeneous mixture.
rubric.description: A homogeneous mixture has uniform composition throughout.
rubric.how: State that its composition is uniform throughout.

rubric.why: Identifies the defining composition of a heterogeneous mixture.
rubric.description: A heterogeneous mixture has non-uniform composition in different parts.
rubric.how: State that its composition is not uniform throughout.

modelAnswer: A homogeneous mixture has a uniform composition throughout; for example, salt solution.
A heterogeneous mixture has a non-uniform composition, with different parts distinguishable; for example, sand and water.
